what_its_for: Pertuzumab is a cancer medicine used to treat a type of breast cancer called HER2-positive breast cancer. It works by attaching to a protein on cancer cells called HER2 and helping your immune system fight the cancer. It is usually given along with another cancer medicine called trastuzumab (Herceptin) and chemotherapy. It may be given before surgery to shrink a tumor, after surgery to lower the chance of cancer coming back, or for breast cancer that has spread to other parts of the body.
how_to_take: Pertuzumab is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it is slowly injected into a vein through a needle or catheter. A nurse or doctor will give you this medicine at a clinic or hospital. Your first infusion will take about 60 minutes. If you tolerate it well, future infusions may take about 30 to 60 minutes. You will be watched closely for at least 60 minutes after your first infusion and 30 minutes after later infusions to make sure you do not have a reaction.
dosing: The usual starting dose is 840 mg given as your first infusion. After that, you will receive 420 mg every 3 weeks (21 days). Your doctor will decide the exact dose and schedule based on your treatment plan. Do not miss or skip any scheduled infusions. Pertuzumab is always given with trastuzumab and is usually given before your chemotherapy on the same day.
missed_dose: If you miss a scheduled infusion appointment, call your doctor or cancer care team right away to reschedule as soon as possible. Do not wait until your next planned visit. If more than 6 weeks have passed since your last dose, your doctor may need to restart you on the higher loading dose of 840 mg. Never try to give yourself this medicine at home.
storage: Pertuzumab is stored and prepared by healthcare professionals in a clinic or hospital. You do not need to store it at home. The medicine must be kept in a refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C) and must not be frozen or shaken. Once mixed for infusion, it should be used right away or stored in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor about all medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take before starting pertuzumab. Avoid becoming pregnant while taking this medicine and for at least 7 months after your last dose, as pertuzumab can harm an unborn baby. Use reliable birth control during treatment and for 7 months afterward. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine and for 7 months after your last dose. Let your doctor know before any surgery or dental procedures.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience any of the following: shortness of breath, trouble breathing, chest pain, or a fast or irregular heartbeat (these may be signs of heart problems); swelling of your ankles or legs; sudden weight gain; fever, chills, or signs of infection; severe allergic reactions such as hives, rash, itching, dizziness, or swelling of the face, lips, or throat during or after your infusion; diarrhea that is severe or does not go away; unusual bleeding or bruising; or if you think you may be pregnant. Also tell your doctor if you feel unusually tired or notice any new or worsening symptoms.
when_it_works: Pertuzumab starts working right away after your first infusion, but it may take several weeks or months before you or your doctor can see the full results. Your doctor will do regular tests, including heart function tests (called echocardiograms or MUGA scans), blood tests, and imaging scans to check how well the treatment is working and to monitor your health. Be patient and keep all of your scheduled appointments.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do not use pertuzumab if you are pregnant. It can cause serious harm or death to an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 7 months after your last dose. If you become pregnant during treatment, tell your doctor right away. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed during treatment or for 7 months after your last dose. Heart problems: Pertuzumab can weaken the heart. Your doctor will check your heart function before and during treatment. Tell your doctor if you have ever had heart disease or heart failure. Elderly patients: Older adults may use this medicine but may need closer monitoring for side effects. Children: Pertuzumab is not approved for use in children.
